metadata.note: cli-explainer spine, weekly work report, claude-hai channel. Episode 7, from the last pushed commit on fix/conformance-skip-list (fbd30b6; origin contains it and the branch is in sync). FRAMEWORK: three questions for any passing check — WHAT DID IT OPEN / WHY IS EACH EXCLUSION THERE / HOW WOULD YOU KNOW IF IT STOPPED. Falsifiability beat is B08: the surface counts were reproduced from the committed tree by re-implementing both versions of the skip rule, and four of five claims matched exactly while the commit message's “zero Python” turned out to be 39 files of one subsystem. The correction is the author's own commit message. See FACTCHECK.md for the recount script.

beats.role_note: series continuity — episode 6's Did-not-test entry, chased down to its cause
beats.narration_text: Episode six listed ten things the attestation had not tested. One of them was that there is no independent test suite and CI runs none of it. That was true, and I had not asked the obvious follow-up: the repository does have a conformance checker, and it was passing. So what was it checking?
beats.new_visual_element: last episode's entry, and the question it should have provoked

shot.show: episode 6's Did-not-test line above, and the unasked question below
shot.visual_intent: A bordered card at the top holds the quoted Did-not-test entry in soft ink. Beneath it, a second bordered card in terracotta holds the question. A short connector runs between them.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions for any passing check, shown AS A STRUCTURE before the evidence
beats.narration_text: Three questions for any automated check that is passing. One: what did it actually open — count the files, by type, not by trust. Two: why is each exclusion there — is it excluded for what it is called, or for where it lives. Three: how would you know if it stopped working. Break it on purpose and see whether it says so.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: WHAT DID IT OPEN / WHY IS EACH EXCLUSION THERE / HOW WOULD YOU KNOW
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered cards land in a row, one per narration step. The first lands in terracotta — it is the question that broke this one open — and the rest of the reel is scored against all three.

beats.narration_text: The ask was to make the checker read the code it claims to check, without making it so slow that nobody runs it.

shot.show: the composer with the conformance ask

props.command: claude "make conformance read the step scripts — and keep it fast enough that people still run it"
props.segment: The ask · read the code, stay fast

beats.role_note: QUESTION 1 — what did it open. Recounted from the committed tree, both versions.
beats.narration_text: Question one. The old run opened a hundred and eighty-seven files. The new one opens seven hundred and forty-three. The difference is four hundred and seventy-six Python files — the executable surface of ninety-nine recipes. Every step script the pipeline runs was outside the checked set, which means two pull requests passed continuous integration without anything compiling a line of their code.

shot.visual_intent: Two bordered columns, before and after, each a stat card with its file count. Between them a terracotta card carries the 476 figure and the words 'executable surface of 99 recipes'. The citation strip names the two commits the counts were reproduced from.

beats.role_note: ACTUAL-CODE LAW — the skip list before and after, from the committed file
beats.narration_text: The fix is not deleting the entries. Three of those names were fine; the problem is that a basename rule skips every directory with that name, anywhere in the repository. Data needed skipping in two places and keeping in two others. So it splits: a name list for things that are never source, and a prefix list for things excluded by where they sit.
beats.new_visual_element: the skip list, split in two

shot.show: the old single skip list and the new two-list split, verbatim

props.title: scripts/conformance.mjs  @ fc645e8
props.sparkLine: A basename rule cannot say “only this one”

beats.role_note: the speed trap — and the silent fallback that hid it
beats.narration_text: Deleting the entries alone made it eleven times slower: six seconds to sixty-three, because it spawns one interpreter per file. A check nobody waits for stops being run, so the calls are batched. But batching has a trap. Windows command lines cap at eight thousand one hundred and ninety-one characters, not the thirty-two thousand usually quoted, so past about a hundred and fifty paths the spawn failed, the code fell back to one file at a time, and the speed-up disappeared while everything still passed. Chunks are capped well under the limit. Final result: four times the files, and faster than before.
beats.new_visual_element: the speed path, and the silent fallback

shot.visual_intent: Three bordered bars in a row showing the three timings, the middle one tallest and in soft ink, the last shortest and terracotta. Beneath, a short labelled axis marks 6000 (the cap used) and 8191 (the real limit) with the region past it marked 'spawn fails, falls back, still passes'.

beats.role_note: QUESTION 3 — break it on purpose. The five checks from the commit.
beats.narration_text: Question three. Five things were broken on purpose to see whether the checker noticed. A syntax error appended to a step script: caught and named. A truncated run envelope: caught and named. Quarantined and private files: zero leaked in. A file named explicitly inside a skipped tree: still checked. And the deliberately broken JSON fixtures stayed invisible, because those are supposed to be broken.
beats.new_visual_element: the five break tests, each with its expected result

shot.show: 5 rows: what was broken, and what the checker did
shot.visual_intent: Five rows, each a drawn tick beside a monospace label, landing one at a time. The fourth and fifth sit in a bordered terracotta box — they are the two that prove the exclusions behave, rather than that the checker merely runs.

beats.role_note: THE RECOUNT — the commit message overstates by 39 files, and the recount catches it
beats.narration_text: Now the part that matters. Episode six's rule was to recount every figure from the file rather than trust the commit message. I did that here. A hundred and eighty-seven, seven hundred and forty-three, four hundred and seventy-six, ninety-nine recipes — all four reproduce exactly. One does not. The message says the old run checked zero Python. It checked thirty-nine: one subsystem, and mostly that subsystem's own tests. No recipe step script, which is the claim that actually matters — but the headline number is wrong, and it is my commit message.
beats.new_visual_element: five claims recounted, four green and one corrected

shot.visual_intent: Five rows, each a claim with a recounted value beside it. The first four carry drawn ticks in ink. The fifth carries a terracotta cross and the corrected figure, with a small bordered note naming scripts/gateway as the whole of it.

beats.role_note: the companion commit — why hashes only count if they reproduce off this machine
beats.narration_text: The second commit on the branch is the reason any of this can be evidence. Recipe reports cite the hash of every script they ran, but Git was storing one line ending and checking out another, so a file's hash changed with the machine. Line endings are now pinned repository-wide, with shell scripts forced to the one ending that keeps a shebang readable. Twenty-one hundred and twenty files normalised, and two hundred and fifty sampled at random — all two hundred and fifty now hash identically to what is committed.
beats.new_visual_element: the hash problem, and the pin that fixed it

shot.show: the same file hashing two ways, then the pin, then 250 of 250
shot.visual_intent: Left: one file icon branching to two different hashes, in soft ink, with the branch struck in terracotta. Right: a bordered panel with the pin rules and the 250/250 result. The citation strip names the .gitattributes commit.

beats.role_note: scaffolded task — the rubric on the viewer's own CI, with a GOOD/BAD discriminator
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Open whatever check guards your project and make it print what it opened — not whether it passed, but the count and the file types. Then compare that against what you believe it covers. The gap is the part nobody is checking.
